en: Catalogue of the Vows of Upāsikās:
Pang Xingpo, Lingzhao Nü,
Jiancha Po, and Ling Xingpo.
Madam Li; Madam of Mount Tai;
Madam Who Turns the Canon; Madam of the Single Palm;
Madam Who Is Speechless; Madam Who Plants the Rice Paddies.
The laywoman Ba-lin, the nun Zheng Shisan-niang,
the resident of the hermitage Po-ping-tian, and Sister Bi-men-po.
The Old Woman of Fenglin; the Old Woman Who Sold Cakes;
the Old Woman Who Threw Away Her Child; the Wife of Ganqi;
Master Cui; and the Old Woman Chen Dao.
Yudao Po, Shaoyuan Po, Xingqian Po,
Juean Zu, Daoren Ming, Lingren,
and Lady Fan of Fan County.
The Biographies of Upāsikās, concluding with the Table of Contents for the *Qinguo furen Shen Daopo* (Lady Shen Daopo of the Qin State).
Edited by the Elder Fēng of Jìngshān, Yuánxìn;
verified by Wúdìdì Zhǔrén, Guō Níngzhī; compiled by Páng xíngpó.

The laywoman Pang Xing entered Lukmen Temple to offer a vegetarian feast. When the *vina* (chant leader) requested her intention for the dedication of merit, the laywoman took up a comb, stuck it behind her hair-knot, and said, "The dedication has been made.
She then departed. Later, when it was heard that the layman and Lingzhao had passed away together, she remarked: [This refers to their simultaneous departure.]
"This foolish woman and that ignorant old man have departed without even bidding farewell! How can this be endured? Thinking thus, she went to inform her son.
Upon seeing him clearing the fallow field, she said, "Master Pang and Lingzhao have gone! Her son dropped his hoe and responded, "Huh? After a long while, he too stood up and vanished.
His mother cried out, "How extremely foolish and deluded my son is! She, too, had him cremated. The multitude [grieved].
Everyone marveled at this. Before long, the nun Xing took leave of her fellow villagers by visiting them all and retired into seclusion.
Thereafter, she vanished from sight entirely, and no one knew where she had gone.
Lingzhao was the daughter of Layman Pang. One day, when Danxia came to visit the Layman, he saw Lingzhao washing vegetables.
Danxia asked, "Is the Layman at home? Lingzhao set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands clasped. Danxia asked again.
"Is the Layman at home? Lingzhao took up her basket and went straight away. Upon her return, she reported this to the Layman.
The Layman said, "Red earth smeared on a cow's udder. While the Layman was sitting with the old nun and Lingzhao, the Layman said, "Difficult, difficult, difficult!
Ten piculs of sesame oil spread across the top of a tree. The Nun said, "Easy, easy, easy! The meaning of the Patriarchs upon the tips of the hundred grasses. Lingzhao said:
"It is neither difficult nor easy; when hungry, one eats; when tired, one sleeps.

The layman asked, "As for the saying, 'Clearly bright at the tips of the hundred grasses, clearly bright is the meaning of the Patriarch'—how do you understand this? Lingzhao said, "You are old and decrepit, yet you speak such words.
The layman asked, "How about you? Lingzhao said, "Clearly bright at the tips of the hundred grasses, clearly bright..."

The Patriarch Ming expressed his intention. The layman (Dongshan Liangjie) then laughed heartily. Once, while they were crossing a bridge together under a willow tree selling bamboo sieves, they both tumbled down.
When Lingzhao saw this, she also fell to the ground. The layman asked, "What are you doing? Lingzhao replied, "Seeing my father fall, I am helping him up.
When the layman was about to enter nirvana, he said to Lingzhao, "Observe the sun to see how late it is; report to me when it reaches noon."
Zhao went out the door and immediately announced, "The sun has already reached its zenith, yet it is being eclipsed; you may try to observe it for a moment.
The Layman asked, "Is there such a thing? She replied, "There is. The Layman rose from his seat and leaned over the window, while Lingzhao remained seated cross-legged upon her couch.
He suddenly passed away.
Jiancha, Lama Gu, and Nanquan—these three together went to visit Jingshan. On the way, they encountered an old woman and asked her, "What is the road to Jingshan?"
"Where are you going? the old woman asked. Mazu said, "I am going straight ahead. Mazu asked, "The water ahead is deep; will you be able to cross it?
The old woman said, "My feet will not get wet. He asked again, "The rice on the upper bank is so lush, while the rice on the lower bank is so frail."
The old woman said, "It has all been eaten by crabs. She asked again, "Is the grain fragrant? The old woman said, "It has no scent.
She asked again, "Where do you live, old woman? The old woman said, "I am right here. The three men arrived at the shop;
the old woman brewed a pot of tea and brought three cups with her, saying, "If you monks possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), then drink the tea. The three men looked at one another...
As he was looking on, the old woman said, "Watch as this old crone displays her own supernatural powers. Thereupon, she picked up the tea bowl, poured out the tea, and walked away.

(Hanshan’s commentary says: "Where does the path of Jinshan go? Straight ahead. Let that be for now. As for this fellow who follows the crowd like a white-clad boor—if he had some sense of depth and shallowness underfoot, recognized good and evil with his eyes, or distinguished fragrance from stench with his nose, then upon encountering the old woman pointing out a place to stay, he would have sought his own spiritual powers.

At that moment, he would have lightly brushed aside the tea kettle, flung it over, and walked off. He would have seen how the old woman had reduced their conversation to a single cup of tea, yet [he remained there]. )

What is this "killing by combination"? Do you still understand the old woman? Is she wasting her days in vain busyness, playing with such losses? A sword leaves its precious scabbard because of injustice; medicine emerges from its golden jar because of illness. He sings: "In this shop, no guest is ever let go; for even a drop of water, I swear never to overcharge.
If one can know the true flavor when it is poured out, the entire universe is contained within a cup of tea.
Lingxingpo, Lingxingpo, came to pay her respects to Master Fubei (a Dharma heir of Mazu). The Master offered her a seat and tea. The nun then asked:
"To whom can this phrase, which cannot be grasped even by exhausting one's full strength, be entrusted? The Master said, "Fubei has no superfluous words.
The Lady said, "Before reaching Fubei, I was not without doubt. The Master said, "If you have another point of excellence, feel free to bring it forth.

The Lady folded her hands and wept, saying, "In the midst of heaven, further misery is added to my grievance. The Master was speechless. The Lady said, "Your words do not distinguish between the biased and the correct."
In principle, it is not that he failed to recognize the perversion; rather, when one acts for others, calamity arises. Later, a monk related this to Nanquan, who said, "How bitter!
Fupei has been brought low by this old woman. When the old woman later heard of this, she laughed and said, "Master Wang still lacks a certain skillful means.
A Zen traveler named Chengyi encountered the old woman and asked, "What is it that Nanquan still lacks?"
Yi said, "There is still a slight mechanism remaining. Ba then wept, saying, "How tragic!
How painful! I am utterly at a loss. Yi asked, "Do you understand? Ba joined her palms and stood there. Yi reported this to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, "Had I seen this stinking old woman, I would have questioned her until her mouth was gagged. Yi asked, "I wonder, Master, how would you have handled it?"

He asked another monk, who immediately struck him. One monk said, "Why did you strike me? Zhaozhou replied, "For a fellow like this dead thing, if I do not strike you now, when shall I wait for the time to do so?
He struck him several times in succession. Upon hearing this, the old woman said, "Zhaozhou deserves to receive a blow from my hand.
Later, a monk reported this to Zhaozhou, and Zhaozhou wept, saying, "How tragic! How painful! When the old woman heard of this...

He spoke. Joining his palms, he sighed in praise, saying, "Zhaozhou’s eye shines forth, piercing through the four worlds. Zhaozhou then instructed a monk to ask, "What is Zhaozhou’s eye? The nun then held up her fist. When the monk returned, he reported this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou then composed a verse, saying: The nun holds up her fist; The fist is Zhaozhou’s eye. If you wish to see it clearly, Look at my fist. Zhaozhou then said to the monk, "Did you see it? The monk replied, "I saw it. Zhaozhou struck him. The monk later told the nun, "The Master has hit me. The nun said, "I knew he would strike you. Zhaozhou heard of this and remarked, "This old woman is truly difficult to handle. The nun then composed a verse, saying: Zhaozhou’s eye is truly wondrous; It pierces through the four worlds. When the monk asked about it, I held up my fist. The Master of Zhaozhou was so bold That he struck the monk. The monk returned and told me, "I have been hit by the Master. I said, "I knew he would strike you. The Master heard of this and said, "This old woman is indeed difficult to handle. I then composed a verse: Zhaozhou’s eye is truly wondrous; It pierces through the four worlds. When the monk asked about it, I held up my fist. The Master of Zhaozhou was so bold That he struck the monk. The monk returned
"Directly confronting the situation, he brings it forth face-to-face; directly confronting the situation, the response is swift. I tell you, Laywoman Ling: why this weeping? Why this gain and loss?
The laywoman replied with a verse: "The weeping, the Master has already understood; now that it is understood, who is there to know? At that time in the kingdom of Magadha..."

"How many times has he lost the opportune moment before his eyes? (Hanshan’s critique says: "When one knows few things, afflictions are few; where one recognizes many people, disputes are many. According to Zhaozhou’s initial 'ordinarily there is nothing' (*pingchang wushi*) division, he was truly a resolute man.

Yet at the end, he again suppressed the head of the case and added a few more words—this can be called losing money and then suffering punishment, with the guilt extending to the roots and branches. What a grievance! What suffering! Nevertheless, the old woman did not have good intentions either; she was much like someone clutching stolen goods while crying out for injustice.)

In the end, how can one fully express this principle? Heaven! Heaven! What I offer is the truth. He cried out: "Silence meets death as they vie for supremacy; with celestial eyes he gazes afar, emitting great radiance. To urge the old woman to cease her vain weeping—how few know the pain that wells from the very core!"
As for Master Changzi Kuang of Tanzhou and Li Xingpo: When Li Xingpo came, the Master asked, "Do you remember the events when we were in Jangzhou?
She replied, "If it were not for you, Master, I would not know. The Master said, "Much is empty and little is real. She said, "What is there to hide?"
At that place, the Master said, "I am mindful that you are a woman; I let you go with your staff. The old lady said, "I, this humble person, never see any fault in a venerable elder.
The Master asked, "Where does the old monk’s fault lie? The old lady said, "If the Master has no fault, how could I possibly have one?
The Master asked, "What is it like for one who has no fault? The old lady then held up her fist and said, "To act thus is entirely madness."

[The monk] fell over. The Master said, "Truly, there is no place to hide. [Han-shan’s critique says: "Alas! This worldly teacher has white hair and broken teeth, yet he still sees faults in others. Though the old woman is female, her poisonous fist stands alone;

she can both grant and snatch away. How could this master not know how to conceal himself? He has taken up the cangue and the indictment all by himself. Furthermore, he wields his blind staff in reverse—how great a humiliation! In the end, how can he vindicate himself? It is easier to turn a speck of stone into gold and jade than it is to persuade people to abandon their right and wrong.
He sings: 'A lone dog barks at the void; a thousand monkeys gnaw at reality. To bend the straight into a curve—who shall eat the blow from the staff? "
There was an old woman at Mount Tai. A monk traveling to the Five Terraces Mountains asked an old woman, "Which way does the road to Mount Tai go?
The woman said, "Go straight ahead. The monk then departed. The woman said, "What a fine monk, yet he goes away like that. Later, another monk recounted this story.
He resembled Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Wait until I go and examine her. The next day, Zhaozhou went and asked, "Madam, which way does the road to Mount Tai go?
The old woman replied, "Go straight ahead. Zhaozhou then departed. The old woman said, "What a fine monk, yet he goes away like that!
Zhaozhou returned to the monastery and told the monks, "The old woman of Mount Tai has been thoroughly exposed by me for your sake. (Xuange said: The former...)

When the monk spoke thus, Zhaozhou also spoke thus. Wherein was the point where he exposed the old woman? It is further said: "Not only was she exposed by Zhaozhou, but she was also exposed by this monk. Xuedou Xian went to the residence of Scholar Zeng.

Zeng asked, "I have often discussed with Elder Qing the story of Zhaozhou exposing the old woman. Is there, in truth, a point where she was exposed? Xuedou said, "What did Elder Qing say? Zeng said, "He also went off in that way. Xuedou said: [Silence].

Yunmen said, "Old man Qing, let this one matter pass for now. Does the Academician know that the monks of the world cannot escape the snare of this old woman? Zeng once said, "There is another way here. Had Zhaozhou not exposed the old woman’s trickery, [the matter would have remained unresolved].

[The monk] spent his whole life being humiliated. [Zhaozhou] said, "I have seen through you. (Zhenjing said, "If Zhaozhou had examined him closely, he too would have deserved a blow from the old lady’s staff. But tell me, where did Zhaozhou go wrong? If you know where Zhaozhou went wrong, only then will you understand how not to be deceived.

Is there anyone under Guizong who is not deceived? [He let out a shout and descended from the seat]. (Jingshan Daokai’s verse: The world’s Chan practitioners talk of 'seeing through'; who knows that Zhaozhou has already fallen into words? [He cited...]

"Having obtained sons and grandsons, one is no longer a man of stature; everyone points at him as he lies on the cold ground. (Mong-an Yue’s verse: "Originally a man of the mountains, I love to speak of mountain talk. Selling 'pine-wind' in the fifth month—fear it has no price in the human world. (Gao-feng picks up [the case] and says:

"Regarding this public case, if judged according to the various quarters, Zhaozhou has seen through the old woman. But if examined by Gao-feng, it is precisely the old woman who has seen through Zhaozhou. Ultimately, what serves as the proof? He points with his finger.)

[The Master] said, "Go straight ahead. The verse says: "From childhood, it could not be captured by brush and ink; Only in recent years has one realized the art is truly refined. Casually casting down the brush, it becomes a dragon and departs;

It changes the pupils in the eyes of people of this age. Yufeng Xin added: "On the road to Mount Tai, one cannot do without this old woman. Since Zhaozhou exposed her, until the present day, the grass has grown tall and wild, falling eastward and collapsing westward. The verse says: 'Mount Tai’s old woman, Mount Tai’s old woman! When dead, she is utterly beyond help.'"

"Opening one's eyes to let others pierce the nostrils; an evil person naturally has an evil person’s demon. (Hanshan’s commentary says: "If you wish to know the road beneath the mountain, first ask those who have already traveled it. Let us set this monk aside for a moment—do you yet recognize Zhaozhou’s point of arrival?

Just now he was too talkative, and by seeking the path to Tai Mountain as before, he has already missed the eight thousand [li] by far. He sings: "A vast, ancient road, traversed even before the mother was born. Without cause, the old fellow dropped his words, only to be exposed by the old woman.")

There was a woman from a village who sent someone with money to request that the Tripitaka be recited. After Zhaozhou had accepted the offering, he descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated it once, and said, "Deliver this message to the woman:
the recitation of the Tripitaka is finished. When the messenger returned, he reported this to her.
The nun said, "I have recently requested that you turn the entire Tripiṭaka; why do you only turn half of it? (Xuánjué said: "Where is it that half the Tripiṭaka is missing?

Tell me, what kind of eye does that nun possess to speak in such a manner? (Jìngshān Gǎo said: "Among the assembly, some deliberate on this by asking, 'What is that half of the Tripiṭaka? Some say to circle [the stūpa] once more; some snap their fingers;

some cough; some give a shout; some clap their hands. Such a view is simply a lack of shame. As for that half of the Tripiṭaka, let alone saying that Zhaozhou should circle once more—even if one were to do so hundreds, thousands, ten millions, or billions of times...")

"Even if one were to circumambulate [Mount Sumeru] a hundred thousand million times, at the old woman's share, one would still only obtain half a *piṭaka*. Even if the Old Monk of the whole world were to circumambulate it together with you like this a hundred thousand million times, at the old woman's share, he too would only obtain half a *piṭaka*.

Even if the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the myriad phenomena of the forest, and every blade of grass and tree were each to possess the mark of the broad and long tongue, speaking with one voice in unison from this day until the end of the future, at the old woman's share, they too would only obtain half a *piṭaka*.
Do you all wish to recognize the old woman? (After a long silence) He said: 'The embroidered mandarin ducks are finished; look for yourself. I do not hand the golden needle over to others.'"

Chu Shi Qi said: "This old woman claimed that Zhaozhou only turned the *Prajñāpāramitā* in fifty-six thousand eight hundred verses, playing with the false to represent the true. At that time, she should have simply said: 'Why did you not realize it before you walked around the meditation seat? Han Shan’s commentary says: "Five thousand, six thousand, eight."

Prajñe-pāramitā. If one were to complete the Great Canon, it would not take more than a single breath; yet there is neither whole nor half, as it turns upward and downward. Heaven is dark-blue and earth is yellow—how vast, how profound! He cried out: "One character per day is not a small amount; one circuit of the Canon is merely too much.
Old age leaves me without the strength to leave my bed; wherever I receive money, I must spend it."
A Palm: Zhaozhou asked an old woman, "Where are you going? She replied, "I am going to steal Zhaozhou’s bamboo shoots. Zhaozhou said, "What will you do when you encounter Zhaozhou?
The woman then gave him a slap, and Zhaozhou desisted. (Hanshan’s commentary says: "How amusing! This radiant piece of Zhaozhou...")

There was not even a single blade of grass on the ground. To openly entice a thief into the gate is precisely like being caught red-handed with stolen goods and receiving a beating. If the Governor had waited for him to clap his hands, he would have suddenly cried out, "Thief! Thief! and forced him to suffer the full penalty. This is the failure of his life. He then proclaimed: [The text ends here.]

House after house, jade tablets pierce through the forest; turning one's back on others, one secretly commits a fraud. Had one not encountered the master, one would have first awakened oneself; with a single fist, one breaks through Zhaozhou’s barrier.
The monk Wuye was once traveling when he encountered an old woman on the road. The woman asked, "Where does the Master reside? Zhaozhou replied, "West of the East Courtyard of Zhaozhou.
The woman was left speechless. Upon returning, Zhaozhou asked the assembly of monks, "Which character for 'west' should have been used? Some said: [text truncated]
"Characters for 'east' and 'west,' or as some say, characters for 'resting and dwelling. Zhaozhou said, "All of you would make excellent salt-and-iron commissioners.

They asked, "Why do you speak thus, Master? Zhaozhou said, "Because you all know how to read characters. (Fadeng’s variant says: "They already know where they are headed. (Hanshan’s commentary says: "Fundamentally there is no place to dwell;

one dwells in this very way. Everyone has their own place of dwelling. Why is it that this old woman, despite being so clear-headed, remains utterly ignorant? She stands at a three-way fork, beating her drum.)"

Two pieces of skin; he asks only about the affairs within that man’s house. His heels do not even touch the ground. When he sees him pointing east and drawing west, there is no trace of substance at all. Why did he remain silent without uttering half a word, causing the toothless old man to shrink back his mouth?

He ought to have said: "I have long heard of Zhaozhou; it turns out he is merely smearing things here and there. This would have forced him to stop his rambling east and west, leaving him with a dry, dull, and frustrated field of experience—only then would one be a remarkable female general.

It would have resulted in nothing more than a large head and a pointed tail. One must present the sword when meeting a swordsman; unless you are a poet, do not offer a poem. He sang: "Each person must support their own collapsing house; why wait for a lowly, servile scoundrel? The four quarters remain as they were before. Zhaozhou.
(Hanging a gourd on the eastern wall).
While Zhaozhou was out in the fields, he saw an old woman planting rice and asked her, "What would you do if you suddenly encountered a fierce tiger? The woman said:
“There is not a single dharma that can be taken as an object of the mind. Zhaozhou said, “Hmph! Ba also said, “Hmph! Zhaozhou said, “There is still this one remaining. [Hamshan’s Commentary]:

When the wood is small and everything is empty, the mind alone becomes a tiger. Why, under the clear blue sky and bright sun, amidst shallow grass and sparse forests, do you fail to bring up these plain and straightforward words? Instead, you cause those who should be planting fields to sow wild rice.

"Deliberately eating at this scene, one is startled and amazed. Yet, there is still the tiger; there is still the person. Departing from these two paths, I ask you to speak otherwise. The Layman then made a fist and assumed the posture of two tigers wrestling, saying:

"Last night, the white-jawed beast of the South Mountain bit off the scorched tail. With a sudden flash of silence, it was precisely the right news. With a single long啸 (shout of joy), he vanished into the deep mist, straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags. He sang: "No dharma can withstand the mind; what fear, then, what hindrance? Niu-tou was not the Fourth Patriarch—yet even now, this very thing remains."
There was an old woman who came to lodge. As evening fell, she entered the monastery, and Zhaozhou asked, "What are you doing? The woman replied, "I am seeking lodging.
Zhaozhou said, "What kind of place is this? The woman let out a great laugh and departed. (Hanshan’s commentary says: Once there was a man of vision...)

When women were clamoring as they toured the temple, the Master looked at his disciples and asked, "The sound of hairpins and bracelets can be heard through the wall; even by the Vinaya standards, this is called breaking the precepts. How do you propose to handle this right now? His disciples then spoke with composure, saying, "This is a most excellent way in. It would be fortunate for future generations if this precedent were established.

The Master said, "This centenarian—hair white and teeth fallen out—has only recently encountered this old woman seeking a place to stay. The monk said, "If that is so, then what is the meaning of the teachings on cause and effect, retribution, and the three realms of existence? The monk said, "If they are not ultimate reality, then what is ultimate reality? The nun said, "Ultimate reality is like space—vast, boundless, and without center or periphery. It cannot be grasped, cannot be described, and is beyond all words and thoughts. If you seek it through the senses or the intellect, you will wander further and further away. The monk bowed and withdrew. The nun said, "Do not forget this. The monk departed. The nun called out after him, "Monk! Do not mistake the Buddha-dharma for worldly things! The monk turned his head and looked back; the nun had vanished. The monk sighed and said, "This woman has indeed seen the Way. He returned to the monastery and recounted the encounter to the assembly. Everyone marveled at her insight. The nun later passed away and was reborn in the Pure Land. Her name was Miaozhuangyan (Adornment of Wonder). The monk was known as Xuedou Chongxian. This story is recorded in the *Xuedou Chanshi Yulu*.
"I do not confuse the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "If you act like this, is that not confusing the Buddha-dharma?

When Linji was traveling to Fenglin, he encountered an old woman on the road. The woman asked, "Where are you going? Linji said, "I am going to Fenglin.

The Old Woman Selling Cakes:

On the road to Liyang there was an old woman who sold cakes. Initially, when Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian was frequently lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he was traveling out of Shu carrying the commentaries and sub-commentaries of Qinglong.
He stopped to rest his shoulders and bought some cakes for refreshment. The old woman then pointed to his pack and asked:
[The Master] said, "What text is this? The Master replied, "The *Qinglong Shuchao* (Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra by Qinglong).

The woman asked, "Which sūtra do you lecture upon? The Master replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman said, "I have a question. If you can answer it, I will provide you with refreshments;
if you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere. She continued, "The *Vajracchedikā* says: 'The past mind is unattainable; the present mind is unattainable...'"

"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. I do not yet know which mind the Venerable Elder is pointing to. The Master remained silent. Layman Pang sent him to Longtan.
After attending upon him for a long time one night, he went out; returning, he said, "It is dark outside. Longtan lit a paper candle and handed it to him.
As the Master reached out to receive it, Longtan blew it out. At that moment, the Master attained great enlightenment. He subsequently burned his commentaries and sub-commentaries at the Dharma Hall.

In front of the hall, it was all the old woman’s instigation. (Hanshan’s commentary says: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. The black cat and the white ox chant the *Prajñāpāramitā* for you until they have completely punctured their bellies.
If there were a man of spirit among them, he would immediately lay down the burden of the dead hawk on his shoulders and burn the dragon’s spittle from Qinglong.

Even if he were to go straight to Longtan, there would be nothing he could do about him. It is a pity that the old woman, with her fervent heart, failed to find anyone to buy it. Enough, enough! Let your literary compositions fill your belly as you will; it remains a painted cake that cannot satisfy hunger. He then sang: "The *Vajra* staff weighs a hundred pounds; the leather bag has no wisdom.")
A single point. It combines with the flame-light of the oil-cake (to wait for a wise person to provide a paper wick).
Pao-erh-po, Master Yan-tou Huo, resided in E-chou. Encountering the suppression of Buddhism, he served as a ferryman by a lake; on both banks...

"I shall not ask about presenting the oars and dancing the rowing poles; tell me, from where did this child in the old woman’s hand come?

She then threw [the child] into the water. (Qianyan Chang said: "This old woman could not, after all, relinquish her own life. Yantou was ill-advised to provoke her; he killed one son and acted according to his own rules.

I would give both of them seventy blows. You Zen adepts, if you think this is unfair, then please pass judgment. Yufeng Xin added: "As for this old woman, had Yufeng been in Yantou’s place, he would have sent both her and the child into the water.")

"May she ensure that mother and child remain together, never parted from their flesh and bone. The verse says: "How could this intention not suffice? A foul old woman flaunting her private treasures. A thousand layers of evil waves swallow the waning moon; ten thousand mountains grieve as white clouds multiply. (Hanshan’s Commentary): "Coming has its source; going has its destination.
At that time, when the old woman asked where the child came from—if one had encountered such a person, they would have immediately raised their oar and sung some 'la-la-li' to rescue this child.

This would not have been muddying the waters. Yet, though he struck it with a single stroke, albeit out of compassion, what could he do since the old woman was unwilling? If you wish to find the old woman's whereabouts, do not rely on mere reunion; why spare the younger son? Boya has grown old."

When Zhong and Qi had died, the mountain remained high and the water flowed on. He sang: "One child, then another child; killing and giving life both depend on him. Without strings, he strikes the wondrous notes—few people know this music."

Ganqi’s wife was the laywoman Ganqi. She cultivated the vows of Samantabhadra and, together with her wife and daughter, all practiced the Way. Once, she invited Yantou to spend the summer retreat at her home.
One day, while Yantou was mending his robes, Ganqi returned from outside and stood upright beside him. Yantou picked up [a needle].
He pricked her with a needle to demonstrate [the point]. Zhi immediately attained realization; laughing, she returned to the hall, put on her robes, and paid her respects.
When the wife saw this, she asked, "Why are you laughing? Zhi said, "Do not ask. The wife said, "Even good things should be known by all.
Zhi then recounted [the incident], and his wife was instantly enlightened. She then said, "Thirty years from now, every time I drink water, I shall choke. This was the nun Fang.

As soon as he finished listening to the words from the side, he also attained sudden enlightenment. (Hanshan’s critique says: The previous case has already been addressed by the ancient masters; yet he further says that Master Huo attained enlightenment through a woman.)

It is not merely that he is superior like a parent; the lives and spirits of all people throughout the great earth have been entirely snatched away by Master Huo with a single needle-stab. When the ancient masters reported it thus, they called it "the Zen of soft leather straps. Why is this? They see only the sharpness of the needle’s point, but do not see the tip of the stab.

Had I pressed down upon him simultaneously, although the physician may have eyes capable of making a dull-witted man bleed, it would still be like ladling out a second helping of foul water—transforming it all into the supreme medicine of *amṛta* (clarified butter)—yet it would only serve as a remedy for a dead horse.

Even if the practitioner were robust enough to forge copper sinews and smelt iron bones, such that his joints were so tight no wind could pass and no needle could pierce them, even if one were to take all eighty-four thousand pores and cut them level, placing them directly before him, look at him! How will he respond?

Where does one begin? Why is this so? One sees only the sharp point of the needle, yet fails to see the keen edge of the awl. Let us set aside this matter for a moment; do you recognize that aperture at the crown of the head? A beautiful maiden of sixteen grows weary of her embroidery; beyond the purple *zhijing* flowers, the yellow oriole warbles.

Who pities those whose hearts are bound by the crisscrossing points of concern? All is entrusted to the moment of stilling the needle and remaining silent. [The chant says: "The thick needle pierces closely; through seven holes and eight apertures, one knows not the deep pain—until it is time to be rightfully executed."

There is no retribution, nor is there anyone who does not give, nor anyone who does not receive, nor anyone who does not repay. This would have surely caused the old monk [Zhaozhou], who sat upon his worn meditation cushion, to be unable to contain his amusement, leading him to watch from the sidelines and offer praise. They stare at one another with fixed gazes. This not only renders the lady dull-witted; it is also a slighting insult to her humble servant. [The Master] sings: "On solid ground, he opens both hands; suspended in empty space, not a single thread hangs.
The Buddhadharma, when grasped, is shallow and near at hand; yet the common folk mistake it for something rare and marvelous.

"Raising my ignorance to burn with fire. If one has long been a veteran of the battle lines, it does not hinder one from bringing down two vultures with a single arrow. Yufeng (語風) picked up the words and said: "Looking at this in a cold light, this old woman was not lacking in spirit.

Originally of the same mother-born flesh, one who is thoroughly elegant does not lag behind. "Eh! he raised [his staff]. Then he gave a shout: "Living or dead? One does not even know that the Yang has returned. Yet you remain thus cold and desolate, making such a departure and arrival at the head of a withered stump.

The Woman Distributing Money: Once there was a laywoman who made offerings. As she entered the hall to distribute money to the assembly of monks according to their seniority, a monk said, "Place one portion before the Holy Monks.

[The Master] said: "Fayan is a loquacious fellow; he only knows how to deceive people in the dark. It would have been enough to make a clay figure sneer. Sneer at what? Present this to the Old Man according to the Dharma. [The Master] sings: 'When meeting people, subtract years; when encountering objects, add money. The Holy Monk has no mouth; let him be as he is, even for a donkey-year.'"
Jue’an Zu Daoren (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Zhaojue Qin):
The nun Jue’an Zu was the niece of You Chayuan of Jianning. From her youth, she resolved never to marry.
He applied himself diligently to the ancestral Way and attained clear understanding upon hearing Yuanwu’s words during a public address.
Yuanwu said, "You must cast away what you have seen before you can attain true freedom. Zu replied with a verse: "The pillar protrudes its horizontal bones; Space brandishes its claws and fangs.

Even if one attains a profound realization, It is still but sand in the eye. (Hanshan’s critique says: This matter requires nothing less than thorough cultivation to avoid falling into the trap; others simply cannot manage it.)

One cannot grasp the Dharma, nor can one grasp that which possesses the Dharma. To be bound by the Dharma is like sticky glue; does it not gather birds only to ultimately damage their feathers? It is better to open the cage and set them free, so they may soar unbound in the air and enjoy the supreme pleasure of flight.

Furthermore, it is like releasing a prisoner who has been rescued and restored to reason, only to have him re-imprisoned in shackles and fetters; as soon as he is allowed to rest, he is liberated from the lines drawn upon the ground. It is also like washing a foul-smelling garment with soap; once it is clean, to dwell on the old filth and attempt to scrub away the stains only increases the vexation. Thus, one should simply let go in an instant.

Light and unburdened, it is like polishing a mirror: by adding a small amount of mercury, its radiance suddenly manifests. Those who are stubborn and ignorant, wishing to test the spiritual power of others, instead cloud their own mirrors. Why not hang them upon a stand to shine constantly, so that what is reflected passes through without lingering, perfect and tranquil?

Furthermore, it is like a treasury and its key-case: when a fool turns the key, he merely exerts himself; when a wise person turns the key, they grasp and release as they please, receiving great enjoyment. Again, it is like a blind child who, fortunately having the gold-scalpel applied, beholds the sun once more; as he counts the objects before him, clarity suddenly arises.
